stories.title: Five of our six pollutant pages were printing random numbers
stories.blurb: For about five months, the PM10, CO, NO₂, SO₂ and O₃ pages on JanVayu showed a table of "live levels" whose numbers were random.

stories.title: What a four-day jump in Delhi's AQI tells you
stories.blurb: Delhi's AQI went from 88 on Friday to 169 on Monday, and the explanation offered was that the monsoon is withdrawing, the winds have dropped, and dust and exhaust are staying up longer.

stories.title: What changed in today's redesign, and what stayed the same
stories.blurb: JanVayu has grown by accretion. Every few weeks something arrives that was not there before, it gets a card, and the card goes on the page below the last one.

stories.title: What JanVayu does that the other Indian air-quality sites do not
stories.blurb: Dr Sarath Guttikunda published a list this month of where to get air-quality data for Indian cities.

stories.title: The workshop is a file now
stories.blurb: JanVayu has offered free workshops since April, and there are now four: a tour of the platform, an RTI clinic, a ward-map session, and one written for teachers.

stories.title: Thirty-three cities are getting cleaner and eleven are not
stories.blurb: Nine days ago we published a post about Delhi called Was It Policy, or Was It the Wind? It explained a problem and then admitted a limit: we could separate a real change in the air from a change in the weather, but only for one city,…

stories.title: Was it policy, or was it the wind?
stories.blurb: Every winter somebody announces that Delhi's air has improved. Every winter somebody else announces that it has not.

stories.title: A new way to read your district's air: the airshed as well as the town
stories.blurb: If you live in Ludhiana and the air is bad, whose fault is it?

stories.title: The dataset that looked like our best predictor, and was a map of the Gangetic Plain
stories.blurb: Someone sent us a link and asked a reasonable question: could we use this on JanVayu?

stories.title: What the air looks like
stories.blurb: Everything else on this site is a number. Thirty-one photographs are not, and we should say why they are here.

stories.title: How to read the JanVayu map
stories.blurb: The map now holds a number for every place in India. That means every place, not only every city: all 983,149 administrative areas the country is divided into, from the 36 states down to the 584,615 villages, and every gram panchayat,…

stories.title: Why JanVayu reports PM2.5 first and AQI second
stories.blurb: At a conference last week, a reader made a point worth acting on: our headline figures often led with AQI, when PM2.5 is the measure that carries the health consequences.

stories.title: We were measuring the wrong green
stories.blurb: Earlier today we published a result that bothered us. We had put surface temperature on all 70,417 of India's municipal ward records (68,596 distinct wards, as corrected below), and green cover alongside it, and the two barely moved…

stories.title: Surface heat on every ward in India, and what it showed
stories.blurb: The map has a new Colour menu. Alongside annual air, you can now shade any boundary by surface heat, and for wards by green cover and built-up share.

stories.title: One map, every boundary in India
stories.blurb: Until yesterday, finding out how polluted your neighbourhood is meant knowing something you should not have to know: whether the place you live is officially a ward or a village.

stories.title: Agartala breathes like the coal belt, and nobody was looking
stories.blurb: India's Northeast is usually described in one breath: hills, forest, clean air. For most of the region that is true.

stories.title: Every capital, and the directory we never read
stories.blurb: This morning we published a post saying West Bengal's municipal wards were not openly available.

stories.title: Ninety-seven cities, ward by ward, and the one we had to go somewhere else for
stories.blurb: If you live in an Indian city, the number you see on the news is a city average. One figure stands in for a few million people and hides what you want to know: whether your neighbourhood breathes worse than the one across the flyover.

stories.title: Every village in India is now on the map, including the ones no one measures
stories.blurb: India's air pollution story is told almost entirely through its cities. Delhi in November.

stories.title: Our maps now show the air your MP answers for, in 39 cities and 543 constituencies
stories.blurb: Until this week, our ward map could show you fifteen cities. If you lived in Patna, Ludhiana, Ghaziabad or Indore, some of the most polluted places in the country, the answer to "how bad is my ward?" was that we did not have the boundaries.

stories.title: Testing the chatbot to make it reliable
stories.blurb: These days we ask chatbots almost everything, sometimes things that matter, like whether the air outside is safe to breathe.

stories.title: You don't need to code to make India's air data better
stories.blurb: People assume there are two ways to help a project like JanVayu: write code or send money.

stories.title: Why JanVayu's mascot is a sparrow
stories.blurb: Meet Vayu Gauraiya: vayu is the air, gauraiya the house sparrow. She is the face of Ask JanVayu, our chatbot, the small watchful friend who greets you when you arrive with a question.

stories.title: Scheduled checks that keep JanVayu accurate
stories.blurb: A platform that holds others to account with numbers cannot let its own numbers go stale. Websites go stale quietly, though.

stories.title: We fact-checked our own site and changed 33 numbers
stories.blurb: JanVayu exists to hold others accountable with numbers, so our own numbers have to be right.

stories.title: A working language switcher, easier access for more readers and a much lighter site
stories.blurb: This week's updates added few new panels. They fixed things that already existed so they work properly, load faster and reach more people.

stories.title: Forecasts, fire maps and the health effects of air pollution beyond the lungs
stories.blurb: Five updates went live over the past few days. Here is what changed and why it helps.

stories.title: Up to 42% of India's PM2.5 forms in the air after emission
stories.blurb: When we picture air pollution, we picture a source: a truck's exhaust, a brick kiln's chimney, a field of burning stubble, a cloud of construction dust.

stories.title: A citation that did not exist: 'Krishna et al.' was really Jaganathan
stories.blurb: A platform that asks for public trust has to give people sources they can open and check. If we say 1.72 million deaths a year, or that a +10 µg/m³ rise brings 8.6% more all-cause mortality, you should be able to read the study behind it.

stories.title: Ask JanVayu can now answer questions about your ward
stories.blurb: We built the Ward Atlas, a map of every municipal ward across 14 cities coloured by air, heat, green cover and built-up area, and at first it lived only on the map.

stories.title: Live and annual readings answer different questions about your ward
stories.blurb: When we built the Ward Atlas, a map that colours every municipal ward of a city by its air, heat, green cover and built-up area, we ran into a question that is easy to get wrong.

stories.title: India's air, ward by ward
stories.blurb: When the news says "Delhi AQI is 320," it hides a good deal. There is no single Delhi.

stories.title: Why the heat in your neighbourhood is also an air-quality question
stories.blurb: On a peak summer afternoon, CSE's analysis of Landsat 8/9 satellite data for Delhi found land-surface temperatures reaching 60.77°C at places such as IGI Airport and barren or unsown land, while the area around the Yamuna hovered near 33°C.

stories.title: How we checked that the site is fast and usable on a phone
stories.blurb: On the day we released six Learning Games and refreshed the May 2026 data, we also did some quieter work: we set up automatic checks on the speed and accessibility of the site, and made several changes you will notice on your phone.

stories.title: Six games for learning about air quality
stories.blurb: JanVayu now has a Learning Games panel with six short, original games, meant for classrooms, RWA meetings, family evenings and ten idle minutes on a phone.

stories.title: Updated numbers for May 2026, and what we have been reading
stories.blurb: We aim to keep a reliable public record of India's air quality, and that means keeping the numbers on the front page current.

stories.title: Cigarette equivalents, city rankings, community sensors and workshops are now on JanVayu
stories.blurb: This week's update is the biggest since JanVayu launched. It adds answers to the question most first-time visitors bring: what is this air doing to me right now?

stories.title: In IQAir's 2025 ranking India's average eased, but Loni is the most polluted city
stories.blurb: On March 24, 2026, IQAir released its eighth annual World Air Quality Report, a global assessment of PM2.5 pollution covering 9,446 cities across 143 countries.

stories.title: Air pollution kills 1.5 million Indians a year, and the Lancet now shows the link is causal
stories.blurb: For years, studies in India showed that higher PM2.5 went with higher mortality. Critics, including some in government, answered that correlation is not causation.

stories.title: Has India's National Clean Air Programme worked?
stories.blurb: In January 2019, India launched the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) and promised to cut particulate matter by 20 to 30 percent across 131 cities by 2024, a goal later raised to 40 percent by 2025-26.

stories.title: What air pollution does to India's children
stories.blurb: Air pollution is a direct threat to children's health in India. Evidence from the past five years shows that polluted air stunts children's growth, harms their brains and shortens some lives before they have properly begun.

stories.title: How farmers burn stubble when the satellites are not looking
stories.blurb: Every October, as the kharif paddy harvest ends across Punjab and Haryana, farmers in the two states set fire to crop residue to clear their fields for winter wheat.

stories.title: Air pollution costs India about $339 billion a year
stories.blurb: India's air pollution is usually described as a health emergency, and it is one. It is also a very large economic loss, bigger each year than the entire GDP of most nations (World Bank, 2023 nominal GDP).
